title: Implementation: Problems and Solutions https://curriculumteamleader.wordpress.com/2024/09/30/implementation-problems-and-solutions/
author: Peter Foster
summary: Aimed at middle and senior leaders, Peter Foster breaks down why school-wide changes falter into two categories: behaviour doesn't change at all, or behaviour changes but doesn't produce the intended effect. For the first, he lists diagnostic questions leaders should ask of their own implementation plan, whether it accounted for how behaviour change actually works, whether staff had chances to practise and receive feedback, whether the timing and framing were right, and warns against mistaking early adoption by compliant staff for genuine success, arguing sceptical staff who push back are actually more valuable for stress-testing an idea. For the second, harder-to-diagnose category, he distinguishes a poorly-identified problem (chasing a trendy initiative because another school is doing it, rather than a genuine, evidenced local barrier to learning) from a correctly-identified problem paired with under-communicated implementation, where the visible behaviour (using booklets, using mini-whiteboards) is present but not producing the intended effect because training never covered the specifics of how to use it well. He closes by warning that over-communication can't compensate for genuinely poor implementation elsewhere, and that leaders may need to loop back to the first category, behaviour that hasn't really changed, to diagnose why a seemingly-adopted change isn't working.
points: Foster splits implementation failure into two diagnosable categories, behaviour not changing at all versus behaviour changing without the intended effect, giving leaders a framework rather than a vague sense that 'it didn't work.'
He explicitly reframes sceptical staff as valuable rather than obstacles, arguing getting only the compliant staff to adopt a change is 'not much of a success' since it hasn't been genuinely tested.

He distinguishes a poorly-identified problem (chasing a trend because another school is doing it) from a correctly-identified problem with under-communicated implementation, arguing leaders often misdiagnose which failure they're actually facing.

His closing warning, that over-communication can't paper over poor implementation, pushes leaders back toward auditing whether staff were actually trained on how to use a new resource, not just told to use it.
quotes: It’s better to implement a mediocre idea well than a great idea badly.
There is probably more in common between plans that fail than we realise. In fact, we could probably reduce the main problems all the way down to two key areas.
It’s not much of a success to get your teachers who will do whatever you ask to make a change. It’s a much harder task to convince those who are sceptical or naturally questioning.
A problem is not simply the gap where you want your desired solution to go. School X is doing Exciting Initiative Y so you decide you should be doing that too.
Mini-whiteboards are present in classrooms; they’re even being used. But mistakes are missed and there is little adaptation to the data coming from students.
Over-communication can’t paper over the cracks of poor implementation elsewhere.
